claims.text: At stage-2 Order has `public Customer? Customer { get; set; }` and `CustomerId { get; private set; }` (set only by the public constructor); DonHangDbContext maps `e.HasOne(o => o.Customer).WithMany().HasForeignKey(o => o.CustomerId)`.
At stage-2 Order.Cancel(), Ship() and MarkPaid() read only Status and Id (for exception messages); none reads CustomerId, Customer or customer data.
At stage-2 OrderItem has `int ProductId` and Payment has `int OrderId`, plain int properties with no navigation property to Product or Order.
EfOrderRepository.FindAsync is `db.Orders.Include(o => o.Items).FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id)`: it loads the order and its items, not the customer; CancelOrderAsync and ShipOrderAsync call it.
EF Core does not load a related navigation (Order.Customer) unless the query asks for it (Include, or lazy loading, which Đơn Hàng does not configure); so FindAsync leaves Customer null.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Loading Related Data (eager loading, lazy loading requires proxies or ILazyLoader)

claims.text: The only stage-2 code following Order.Customer reads it: EfOrderRepository.cs:28 (`o.Customer!.FullName` in Select) and NotificationSender.cs:69-71 (Email, FullName for the email; loaded by NotificationQueue.cs:28 ThenInclude). No code assigns a customer property through an order.
A Select projecting into a non-entity record (OrderSummary) that reads `o.Customer!.FullName` returns no entity instances, so EF Core tracks no Customer.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Tracking vs. No-Tracking Queries (tracking and custom projections)

claims.text: PlaceOrderAsync adds the order, then calls notifier.Send (QueuedNotifier adds a Notification with Status "pending" to DonHangDbContext), then one SaveChangesAsync; CancelOrderAsync and ShipOrderAsync call notifier.Send before their one SaveChangesAsync.
With no explicit transaction, a single SaveChangesAsync applies all its changes in one transaction: either all are saved or none (when the provider supports transactions, as Npgsql/PostgreSQL does).
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Transactions (Default transaction behavior)

claims.text: NotificationSender, a BackgroundService, later claims pending notifications rows (NotificationQueue), sends the email and updates Status/SentAt apart from any order use case. Notification has `Order? Order`, set by QueuedNotifier and read via `notification.Order!.Customer!`.

One transaction for two aggregates fits when losing the second change costs more than coupling the saves (saved separately, the order could be written and its notifications row lost: no email); opposing view: when it can happen later or fail alone, save separately.
claims.source_hint: outline item 5; DDD aggregate design guideline 'modify one aggregate per transaction'

claims.text: Referencing other aggregates by id (not by object) and keeping aggregates small so a use case loads only what its rules need is a guideline of tactical DDD aggregate design, not a rule of EF Core.
claims.source_hint: outline items 1, 4; DDD aggregate design guidance (reference other aggregates by identity)

claims.text: db/schema.sql at stage-2 declares `customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id)` on orders; PostgreSQL rejects an INSERT whose customer_id matches no customers row (foreign key violation).
